newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Former NZ First aide rejects coalition option.
newsitem.headline: Former NZ First aide rejects coalition option.

text.p: Nationalist New Zealand First should reject a coalition with both the National and Labour parties, a former adviser to NZ First leader Winston Peters said in an interview.

NZ First holds the balance of power after the October 12 election and begins its seventh week of talks on Monday with the centre-left Labour and the incumbent conservative National government over the shape of the next government.

"We should stay out of any coalition. NZ First was set up primarily in opposition to both Labour and National. Our standard should always be the policies we were founded on, the policies we promoted during the election campaign," former Peters' aide Terry Heffernan said.
At a rally in his Tauranga electorate on Sunday, Peters indicated NZ First would join a coalition and that a decision on a partner was close.
But Heffernan said NZ First would ensure better accountability outside a coalition.

"If parliament is doing its job and decides the shape of legislation then the executive assume far less importance, are in fact cut down to size. That was what New Zealanders voted for with MMP. A parliament in control. If parliament is doing its job it almost doesn't matter (who is in the executive). Parliament must be supreme," Heffernan said.
Heffernan ran unsuccessfully in the Auckland seat of Albany, and was too low on the party's list to win a list seat.
He was demoted in Peters' office earlier this year shortly after Peters' friend and party strategist Michael Laws left National to join NZ First as Peters' chief adviser.
Heffernan blames the influence of Laws for NZ First not taking the independent option and for other policy shifts.

"Sadly, no I don't (expect NZ First to take the independent option). Because much to my disappointment and almost shock in the last couple of weeks of the campaign Mr Laws was writing the speeches that bespoke a determination to be in government come what may. That raised the question: which of National and Labour will you be supporting? And that was a trap that cost us dearly.

"What we were doing was closing off our options to the extent of removing the option of not being in a government at all, and we lost some of our power and started to worry a great number of our supporters."
Heffernan said he did not know which way NZ First would go because the decision would be made by MPs and the party's council and many would not yet know details of the talks.
"Plainly it is a case of chosing whatever party offers NZ First a greater part of what it campaigned on. If it is not that, then those making the decision are betraying their own party."
He said NZ First should return to policies of accountability and economic nationalism.

"We should be representing, personifying accountablility, transparency, honesty -- the very things Winston Peters fought so long to establish in the public mind. We need somehow to undo the damage done by all the policy u-turns... and get back the reputation for consistency and therefore credibility. That was NZ First's greatest asset."

He said the NZ First Maori MPs winning all five Maori electorate seats was "the only shining star out of the whole election result". NZ First won 13 percent of the vote but its support peaked at about 30 percent in polls early in 1996.
"NZ First's overall result was extremely disappointing compared to where we could have been," Heffernan said.
